doc.title: Jane Jarvis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: No place for women in 1929 jazz; Mary Lou Williams and women's bands
summary: She explains that in 1929 jazz offered women little, recalls listening to Mary Lou Williams and Andy Kirk rehearse, and why she avoided novelty women's bands in favour of radio.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: The big problem in music, is you had to either go to the education formula, or cast your wits against the world in jazz. Because there was no forum, mind you, eighty years ago. Not eighty years ago, well, in 1929 is when all this took place. In 1929, there was no place for a woman to play jazz. Now I was friends with Mary Lou Williams, because she and Andy Kirk were at the Club Alabam, which was right on my way to Bush Conservatory, and I used to sit and listen to the rehearsals. Big bands used to rehearse, you know, in the afternoons. And that’s where I met her.
And Chicago was a pretty happening town for music, right?
Oh at that point, but of course I was too young to go anywhere, but wasn’t it clever of me to get a scholarship at a Conservatory where I could walk right past where Mary Lou Williams was?
So if you did play jazz, there was no place to go unless you could get in with a big band. There were women bands at that time, but that kind of life didn’t appeal to me, and
besides, I wanted to be in a man’s band, see? Because it was more powerful at that point. And women’s bands did not get recognition.
Yeah. They were a novelty. And I didn’t like that. So it was easier for me to go the radio and eventually television route. And then I used my ability to play jazz to earn money other than that.
